title: Zariski-local matrix models for a reductive group of semisimple rank one
statement:
Let $A$ be a nonzero commutative Noetherian ring [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], $S=\operatorname{Spec}A$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum], and $r\geq0$. An $A$-group scheme means a scheme over $S$ with multiplication, identity and inverse satisfying associativity, unit and inverse diagrams, as in [def-sc-group-scheme] with this base in place of a field. Put $T=\mathbf G_{m,A}^r=\operatorname{Spec}A[M]$, $M=\mathbf Z^r$, where $A[M]=A[z_1^{\pm1},\ldots,z_r^{\pm1}]$, $e^m=\prod_jz_j^{m_j}$, and the group law is multiplication of units. Write $\chi_m:T\to\mathbf G_{m,A}$ for the character $e^m$. Let $G$ be a smooth [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] affine finite-type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] $A$-group scheme with a closed inclusion $T\hookrightarrow G$ [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Assume every geometric fibre of $G$ is reductive, meaning connected [def-weil-connected-scheme] with no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent closed subgroup. Unipotent means that all geometric points are unipotent matrices in a faithful representation. Assume $T$ is a maximal torus in every geometric fibre, where a torus over an algebraically closed field is a product of multiplicative groups and maximality is for subgroup inclusion. Assume that every geometric fibre of $G$ has semisimple rank one: its quotient by its largest smooth connected normal solvable subgroup has maximal tori of dimension one; solvable means that successive commutator subgroup schemes become trivial. Let $\alpha\in M\setminus\{0\}$ be a root on every geometric fibre, meaning that the conjugation action of the fibre torus on the tangent space at the identity has a nonzero $\alpha$-weight space [lem-sfb-relative-tangent-weight-base-change]. Then $S$ has a cover by affine open subschemes $S_i$ on each of which, for an integer $s_i\geq0$, the pair $(G_{S_i},T_{S_i})$ is isomorphic as a group scheme with specified torus to one of
$$
(\mathbf G_m^{s_i}\times\operatorname{SL}_2,\mathbf G_m^{s_i}\times D_{\mathrm{SL}}),\quad
(\mathbf G_m^{s_i}\times\operatorname{PGL}_2,\mathbf G_m^{s_i}\times D_{\mathrm{PGL}}),\quad
(\mathbf G_m^{s_i}\times\operatorname{GL}_2,\mathbf G_m^{s_i}\times D_{\mathrm{GL}}).
$$
All groups on the right are over $S_i$. For a commutative $S_i$-algebra $R$, $\operatorname{GL}_2(R)$ is the group of invertible $2\times2$ matrices, $\operatorname{SL}_2(R)$ consists of determinant-one matrices, and $\operatorname{PGL}_2$ is the sheaf quotient of $\operatorname{GL}_2$ by the subgroup of scalar invertible matrices for faithfully flat finitely presented coverings. The groups $D_{\mathrm{GL}}$, $D_{\mathrm{SL}}$ and $D_{\mathrm{PGL}}$ are respectively the diagonal invertible matrices, their determinant-one subgroup, and their images in this quotient. The factor $\mathbf G_m^{s_i}$ is central. The isomorphism can be chosen so that $\chi_\alpha$ is trivial on this central factor and equals the ratio of the two diagonal entries on the matrix factor (the ratio is invariant under scalar matrices in $\operatorname{PGL}_2$). The same chosen isomorphisms remain isomorphisms after every base change. No global constancy of the type among these three cases, no triviality of a root line on all of $S$, and no restriction on residue characteristic is assumed.

source.place: WANTED locally; read online https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/luminysga3smf.pdf . Conrad, Reductive group schemes, Theorem 5.1.8 and proof, printed pp.139-140; upper-root orientation as in the proof of Corollary 5.1.9, printed p.141. Definition 5.1.1 and the Zariski refinement in the proof of Lemma 5.1.3, printed pp.136-137, precede applying Theorem 5.1.8.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-relative-rank-one-central-quotient] to the given $G,T,\alpha$. It supplies the central split torus $K=\ker\chi_{\alpha_0}$, $\alpha=d\alpha_0$, the reductive quotient $H=G/K$ and its split maximal torus $\overline T=T/K$, whose inverse image is $T$. Here $d=1$ or $2$, and the centre of $H$ has rank $d$. Thus [lem-sfb-relative-rank-one-semisimple-models] applies to $H,\overline T$. Restrict to one affine open in its cover and put $K\simeq\mathbf G_m^k$, $k=r-1$. We obtain $H\simeq\operatorname{SL}_2$ if $d=2$ and $H\simeq\operatorname{PGL}_2$ if $d=1$, carrying $\overline T$ onto the indicated diagonal torus. Both lemmas have exactly our smooth affine finite-type, reductive-fibre, maximal-torus and semisimple-rank hypotheses; no triviality of a root line on the original base was used.

source.place: Theorem 5.1.8, first paragraph and first two cases, printed pp.139--140.

proof.text: If $H=\operatorname{SL}_2$, the quotient sequence $1\to K\to G\to\operatorname{SL}_2\to1$ is central and fppf-exact by [lem-sfb-relative-rank-one-central-quotient]. The split torus $K$ is separated and commutative, so [lem-sfb-relative-sl2-central-extension-splitting] gives $G\simeq K\times\operatorname{SL}_2$. Its inverse image of the diagonal torus is $K\times D_{\mathrm{SL}}$ and is $T$ by the quotient lemma. This is the first required pair, with $s_i=k$.

Suppose $H=\operatorname{PGL}_2$ and form the group sheaf $\widetilde G=G\times_{\operatorname{PGL}_2}\operatorname{SL}_2$. The scalar map $q:\operatorname{SL}_2\to\operatorname{PGL}_2$ has kernel $\mu_2$ and is fppf-surjective: a projective matrix lifts fppf-locally to $B\in\operatorname{GL}_2(R)$ by the quotient definition; adjoining $c$ with $c^2=\det B$ gives a finite free faithfully flat rank-two algebra, $c$ is a unit, and $c^{-1}B$ has determinant one. Thus $\widetilde G\to G$ has central kernel $\mu_2$, while $1\to K\to\widetilde G\to\operatorname{SL}_2\to1$ is the pullback of the central fppf-exact sequence in [lem-sfb-relative-rank-one-central-quotient]. By [lem-sfb-relative-sl2-central-extension-splitting], $\widetilde G\simeq K\times\operatorname{SL}_2$. The kernel of its map to $G$ is the graph $z\mapsto(\varphi(z),zI_2)$ for a homomorphism $\varphi:\mu_2\to K$, since its projection to $\operatorname{SL}_2$ identifies it with $\ker q$. The inverse image of $T$ is $K\times D_{\mathrm{SL}}$: in the pullback it is exactly $\overline T\times_{\operatorname{PGL}_2}\operatorname{SL}_2$ together with the $K$-fibres, and $q^{-1}(D_{\mathrm{PGL}})=D_{\mathrm{SL}}$. These are identities of sheaves, checked after local matrix lifts, so the graph quotient recovers $G$ and its specified torus.

source.place: Theorem 5.1.8, pullback diagram and splitting, printed p.140; elementary determinant-normalization check of the scalar covering.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-relative-diagonalizable-character-duality], Zariski-locally $\varphi$ corresponds to $u:\mathbf Z^k\to\mathbf Z/2$. Refine to affine opens on which $u$ is fixed. If $u=0$, the graph is $1\times\mu_2$ and the sheaf quotient is $K\times\operatorname{PGL}_2$, with torus $K\times D_{\mathrm{PGL}}$; here $\operatorname{SL}_2/\mu_2=\operatorname{PGL}_2$ follows from the fppf lifting and kernel calculation in step 3. This is the second required pair, with $s_i=k$. If $u\ne0$, its coefficient vector has a nonzero coordinate modulo two. Swap that coordinate to the first position; for every other nonzero coordinate subtract the first basis vector from that basis vector. These integral changes of basis are unimodular and change $u$ to $(1,0,\ldots,0)$. The same duality turns this basis change into $K\simeq\mathbf G_m\times\mathbf G_m^{k-1}$ with $\varphi(z)=(z,1)$. This case forces $k\geq1$. Thus the remaining pair is $\mathbf G_m^{k-1}$ times the graph quotient of $(\mathbf G_m\times\operatorname{SL}_2,\mathbf G_m\times D_{\mathrm{SL}})$ by $z\mapsto(z,zI_2)$.

source.place: Theorem 5.1.8, last paragraph, printed p.140; explicit elementary basis reduction of the nonzero parity vector.

proof.text: The homomorphism $\mathbf G_m\times\operatorname{SL}_2\to\operatorname{GL}_2$, $(t,B)\mapsto tB$, kills the last graph since $z^2=1$. Its kernel is exactly that graph: $tB=I$ forces $B=t^{-1}I$ and $t^2=1$, hence $t^{-1}=t$. It is fppf-surjective by the same rank-two determinant-square-root extension used in step 3: lift $C$ to $(c,c^{-1}C)$ where $c^2=\det C$. Two lifts differ by the displayed kernel, so its graph quotient is $\operatorname{GL}_2$ as a group sheaf. The image of $\mathbf G_m\times D_{\mathrm{SL}}$ is the whole diagonal invertible torus: apply the same square-root lift to a diagonal $C$; conversely scalar multiples of diagonal matrices are diagonal. All these maps are given by the displayed regular matrix formulas, so the quotient identifications are scheme isomorphisms. This gives the third pair with $s_i=k-1$. The unused $\mathbf G_m$ factors are central in each construction.

source.place: Theorem 5.1.8, final identification of the central pushout with GL2, printed p.140; explicit fppf inverse and diagonal-torus calculation.

proof.text: It remains to orient $\alpha$. On each matrix pair the only nonzero torus characters in its tangent conjugation action are $\beta=\operatorname{diag}(a,b)\mapsto a/b$ and $-\beta$: conjugation sends the off-diagonal matrix units $E_{12},E_{21}$ to $(a/b)E_{12},(b/a)E_{21}$ and fixes the diagonal directions. For $\operatorname{SL}_2$ restrict to trace-zero matrices; for $\operatorname{PGL}_2$, the quotient chart where the first diagonal entry is a unit has the unique scalar-normalized representative $B$ with entries $B_{11}=1$, $B_{12}=x$, $B_{21}=y$, $B_{22}=z$ with $z-xy$ invertible. At the identity its tangent coordinates are $x,y,z-1$; diagonal conjugation scales $x,y$ by $a/b,b/a$ and fixes $z-1$. This proves the asserted weight list directly over every ring, including characteristic two. The central product factors act trivially. The tangent base-change and weight identifications of [lem-sfb-relative-tangent-weight-base-change] therefore imply that the given character $\alpha$ becomes $\beta$ or $-\beta$ on every geometric fibre. By [lem-sfb-relative-diagonalizable-character-duality], morphisms of the split tori are locally fixed maps of character lattices; refine the affine cover so that this sign is fixed. If negative, compose on the matrix factor with conjugation by $w=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ (or its projective image). Direct multiplication gives $w\operatorname{diag}(a,b)w^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(b,a)$, so it reverses the sign and leaves the central factor unchanged. Thus $\alpha$ is the ratio character and trivial on the central factor. For any base change, pull back each chosen map together with its inverse; their two composites remain identities by functoriality. This proves the last clause for arbitrary, including nonflat, base change.
